Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette:
Mateo, at twenty-four, had built a life that was supposed to represent a definitive before and after. His desk on the thirty-second floor of a downtown high-rise, with its dual monitors displaying complex financial models, was a world away from the sun-baked valley where his life had fractured two years ago. The trauma had occurred during a foot patrol in an exposed, bowl-shaped basin. He remembered the heat, the oppressive silence, and then the single, sharp crack of a rifle shot. His friend, Leo, had fallen beside him. The memory of that moment never came as a coherent story. Instead, it arrived in sudden, brilliant pieces that would ambush him during the day: the spray of dust from the impact, the precise shade of blue in the sky, Leo's stunned expression. These fragments were intensely clear and detailed, yet he could never put them in the right order. The moments just before the shot and the chaotic minutes after remained a confusing blur, a narrative he couldn't grasp or file away.

The return to civilian life and his new career as a financial analyst was meant to be a clean break, but the past bled through. The sprawling, glass-walled plaza he had to cross to get to his office building became a source of daily dread. Walking through that wide, open space made his skin crawl, a primal feeling of being exposed and vulnerable that mirrored the terror of the valley. He began taking a ten-minute detour, weaving through side streets just to use a different entrance, a habit that often made him late and drew quiet scrutiny from his manager. He knew it was illogical, but the thought of being a target out in the open was a certainty he couldn't shake. At home, the avoidance was different. His mother would occasionally bring up Leo, trying to share a memory or a moment of grief. Mateo would immediately fall silent, his throat tightening, before making an excuse to leave the room. He could not speak of it, not a single word. Talking about Leo felt like confirming his death, a finality Mateo couldn't bear and a conversation that threatened to unleash the chaotic, vivid pieces of memory he fought so hard to contain.

Over time, a set of grim convictions had taken root. Looking at his colleagues, who talked about weekend plans and dating apps, he felt a profound and permanent sense of separation. He was certain that what had happened to him, and what he had done, had marked him as an outsider forever. He had followed orders to take cover rather than stay with Leo, a decision that played on a loop in his mind. He had come to believe he had acted in a way that went against the very core of who he was, a betrayal of friendship and loyalty that made him feel irredeemable. This sense of personal failure fed a deeper, quieter despair. As he charted financial futures for clients, he could not imagine one for himself. The path ahead felt like a flat, grey expanse, devoid of joy or purpose. He had come to believe, with a chilling certainty, that he had no future. It was this creeping hopelessness, coupled with a formal warning from his boss about his chronic lateness and disengaged attitude, that finally propelled him to seek help. He was terrified of talking about the event, but the fear of losing the fragile civilian life he had so desperately tried to construct had become, for the first time, even greater.
